Average acceleration is **change in velocity divided by time**, and the change is a
**vector** subtraction.
**Step 1 — write the two velocities as components.** Take east as +x and north as +y:
v̄₁ = (5, 0) m s⁻¹ - eastward
v̄₂ = (0, 5) m s⁻¹ - northward
**Step 2 — find the change in velocity.**
Δv̄ = v̄₂ − v̄₁
= (0 − 5, 5 − 0)
= **(−5, 5) m s⁻¹**
**Step 3 — find its magnitude.**
|Δv̄| = √(25 + 25)
= **5√2 m s⁻¹**
**Step 4 — divide by the time.**
a_av = 5√2/10
= √2/2
= **1/√2 m s⁻² ≈ 0·707 m s⁻²** ✓
**Step 5 — find the direction.** The components (−5, +5) are equal in size, one **west**
and one **north**, so the vector points exactly midway between them:
**45° west of north** ✓
**Why the two speeds being equal does not make the acceleration zero.** Speed is
unchanged, but **velocity** is not: the direction has turned through 90° ✓ Any change of
direction is an acceleration, which is the whole point of this question.
**Reading it off the figure.** In Fig. 4(CF).1, OA represents v̄₁ eastward and OB
represents v̄₂ northward. To form v̄₂ − v̄₁ one reverses v̄₁ to give OC (westward) and
completes the parallelogram, giving OD - pointing into the **north-west** quadrant at
45° ✓
**A check by components of the answer.** An acceleration of 1/√2 at 45° west of north has
components
x: −(1/√2) sin 45° = **−0·5 m s⁻²**
y: +(1/√2) cos 45° = **+0·5 m s⁻²**
Over 10 s these change the velocity by (−5, +5) ✓ turning (5, 0) into (0, 5) exactly.
**Reading the distractors.** **½ m s⁻² at 60° west of north** ✗ has neither the right
magnitude nor the 45° symmetry that equal speeds demand. **2 m s⁻²** ✗ is nearly three
times too large. **1/√2 at 30° west of south** ✗ has the right magnitude but points into
the wrong quadrant - south, when the particle has gained northward velocity ✓
∴ 1/√2 ms⁻², 45° west of north.

pradeep|Physics|0|2|Pradeep Physics · Cl.s:
Add the three legs as vectors, component by component.
**Step 1 — set axes.** East is +x, north is +y.
**Step 2 — resolve each leg.**
30 m north: **(0, +30)**
20 m east: **(+20, 0)**
30√2 m south-west: south-west is the unit vector (−1/√2, −1/√2), so this leg is
30√2 x (−1/√2, −1/√2) = **(−30, −30)**
**Step 3 — add the components.**
x: 0 + 20 − 30 = **−10**
y: 30 + 0 − 30 = **0**
**Step 4 — interpret.** The resultant is (−10, 0): a displacement of **10 m due west** ✓
**Why the 30√2 is chosen.** Its components are each 30√2/√2 = **30 m**, exactly
cancelling the 30 m northward leg and overshooting the 20 m eastward leg by 10 m ✓ The
awkward √2 is there precisely to make the arithmetic come out clean.
**A check by retracing the walk.** Starting at the origin:
after leg 1: **(0, 30)**
after leg 2: **(20, 30)**
after leg 3: (20 − 30, 30 − 30) = **(−10, 0)** ✓
The walker ends 10 m west of the start and exactly level with it, having walked a total
path of 30 + 20 + 42·4 = **92·4 m** - displacement and distance are very different here.
**The method that avoids error.** Never add displacements as **lengths**; resolve each
into components, add the components separately, then recombine ✓ The south-west leg is
the only one needing resolution, and 30√2 at 45° gives 30 and 30.
**Reading the distractors.** **28 m south** ✗ has a southward component, but the
north-south components cancel to exactly zero. **14 m south-west** ✗ is roughly
√(10² + 10²), suggesting the south-west leg was resolved with the wrong factor. **15 m
east** ✗ has even the direction reversed: the 30 m of westward travel exceeds the 20 m
eastward, so the net must be **west** ✓
∴ 10 m west.

Note: the printed key gives the second option, 28 m south. Resolving the 30√2 m
south-west leg into (−30, −30) makes the north-south components cancel exactly and
leaves (−10, 0), so the displacement is 10 m west. The key has been corrected to the
third option.

The head of the vector moves along the **arc of a circle**, and the change in its
position vector is the **chord** joining start to finish.
**Step 1 — picture it.** The tail is fixed, so the head stays a distance a from it and
sweeps through an angle α on a circle of radius a ✓
**Step 2 — identify what is asked.** The change in the position vector of the head is
r̄_final − r̄_initial - the straight line from the old head to the new one, that is, the
**chord** subtending angle α at the centre ✓
**Step 3 — find the chord length.** Drop a perpendicular from the centre to the chord. It
bisects both the chord and the angle, giving two right triangles with hypotenuse a and
angle α/2:
half the chord = a sin(α/2)
so
**chord = 2a sin(α/2)** ✓
**Step 4 — confirm with components.** Take the vector initially along the x-axis:
r̄_i = a(1, 0)
r̄_f = a(cos α, sin α)
Δr̄ = a(cos α − 1, sin α)
|Δr̄| = a√(cos²α − 2cos α + 1 + sin²α)
= a√(2 − 2cos α)
= a√(4 sin²(α/2))
= **2a sin(α/2)** ✓
using 1 − cos α = 2 sin²(α/2).
**Checking the limits.**
α = 0: the vector has not moved, and 2a sin 0 = **0** ✓
α = 180°: the head has swung to the diametrically opposite point, a distance **2a**
away, and 2a sin 90° = **2a** ✓
α = 60°: chord = 2a sin 30° = **a** - the side of an equilateral triangle, as it must be ✓
All three check out, which no other option manages.
**Reading the distractors.** **2a cos(α/2)** ✗ gives **2a** at α = 0, though nothing has
moved - fatal. **2a tan(α/2)** ✗ and **2a cot(α/2)** ✗ become **infinite** at α = 180°
and α = 0 respectively, but the head can never be more than 2a from where it started ✓
**The general rule.** The magnitude of the change in any vector of fixed length turned
through α is **2a sin(α/2)** ✓ It is the same formula that gives |Δv̄| in circular motion.
∴ 2a sin(α/2).

Treat the **knot** - the point where the horizontal force is applied - as the body in
equilibrium, and resolve the rope tension into components.
**Step 1 — find the tension in the lower part of the rope.** The 10 kg mass hangs in
equilibrium from the lower section, which is vertical, so that section carries
T_lower = mg = (10)(10) = **100 N**
**Step 2 — look at the upper section.** Above the point of application the rope deviates
by **45° from the vertical** at the roof. Let its tension be T, resolved into
vertical: **T cos 45°**
horizontal: **T sin 45°**
**Step 3 — balance the vertical forces at the knot.** The upward vertical component must
support the full 100 N hanging below:
T cos 45° = 100
**T = 100√2 N**
**Step 4 — balance the horizontal forces.** The applied force F must be balanced by the
horizontal component of T:
F = T sin 45°
= 100√2 x (1/√2)
= **100 N** ✓
**The shortcut.** Dividing the horizontal balance by the vertical one eliminates T
entirely:
F/mg = tan 45°
**F = mg tan θ = 100 x 1 = 100 N** ✓ one line, and it shows at once why 45° is chosen:
tan 45° = 1 makes the horizontal force exactly equal to the weight.
**Why the answer does not depend on where the force is applied.** The question says "at
some point" on the rope ✓ Whatever that point, the section above it must carry the whole
weight vertically and the whole applied force horizontally, so the angle at the roof is
fixed by their ratio alone.
**A check on the geometry.** With F = 100 N and weight 100 N, the resultant pull on the
roof is √(100² + 100²) = **141 N** at **45°** to the vertical ✓ exactly the deviation
stated, confirming the answer.
**Reading the distractors.** **140 N** ✗ is 100√2 - the **tension** in the upper rope,
not the applied force; a very tempting value since it appears in the working. **200 N**
✗ is twice the weight, which would need an angle of 63·4°. **70 N** ✗ is 100/√2, from
dividing where one should multiply ✓
∴ 100 N.
